the establishment of an agency to manage large-scale information systems within the area of freedom, security and justice has long been seen as a practical necessity and will thus be a further step towards smoother processing and use of information within the european union. of course, in carrying out its activities, the agency must meet the highest data protection standards of the european union. the collection of information should also not be accessible to member states not part of the system. as regards the choice of the seat of the agency, i fully support the choice of a single centralised seat, since such a solution is the least costly and will also facilitate the cooperation of the various components of the agency. in conclusion, i am pleased that the european parliament has had the opportunity to play a significant and direct part in the establishment of this agency, and i congratulate my colleague mr coelho.

community legislation on family law is a complex issue, whether it concerns the local jurisdiction of the competent courts or the law applicable in cases of crossborder marriages and the regulation of contact and childcare. however, it does not provide sufficient protection for the persons directly concerned, namely children. as a result, children are often used as a means of settling scores between former spouses or partners. following the letter of the law, there are situations where the courts of the member states allow the separation of the natural links between mother and child. i therefore call on the relevant institutions of the european union to align existing legislation to the greatest possible extent with the protection of the child's best interests, not just through vague escape clauses that are problematically applicable in practice, such as article 12 of the brussels ii regulation. the courts' kind and ethical approach in adjudicating such disputes, especially with regard to the protection of the rights and legitimate interests of the child, is also important.

the treaty of lisbon provides a specific legal basis for the development of the energy policy of the european union, which must be appropriately used to modernise, improve interconnection and adapt the union's energy infrastructure to meet the 2020 energy and climate targets. security of supply and strengthening solidarity between member states in the field of energy can, in my view, also be ensured through cohesion policy. in particular, european territorial cooperation provides new opportunities for cross-border cooperation, for example to link local and regional energy sources and large energy networks. the coordination of energy infrastructure projects at local, regional and european level is a prerequisite for ensuring proper network interconnection and maximising the efficiency of funding, whether from regional or european sources.
the european parliament has already adopted the energy policy concept of the european union and many of the approved measures of the european energy interconnection route are likely to be implemented beyond 2020. nevertheless, a look into the more distant future of the european union's energy infrastructure can certainly be useful. new technologies and new types of energy sources also bring new demands on energy distribution and current networks are not always able to transport new types of energy. therefore, a qualified expert view of the energy infrastructure technologies of the european union after 2020 can be a useful basis for the policy-making of the european institutions, as it will help to create a forecast of the financial capacities to provide the energy potential needed for the economic and economic growth of the european union, especially in the future. from that perspective, i think this concept can be interesting.
we don't care what our energy policy, our energy infrastructure, is going to be in the future. it is clear that competition is developing between some member states in the field of energy policy. this requires continuous improvement and modernisation of our infrastructure. we must try to keep national fragmentation to a minimum. particular attention should be paid to member states that rely on a single provider. i would like to highlight the vulnerability of the central european countries in terms of gas supply. in future, infrastructure development must take this into account to some extent to eliminate this. the north-south link is also showing positive results, which can certainly be considered as progress. we need to build networks that can work effectively, with particular regard to solidarity between member states. the question of savings and energy efficiency may also be key. the european union is particularly dependent on a few energy sources, and we must therefore manage our existing energy resources well. i think it is very important for europe to be able to create a common market, and this report can help us to do that. unfortunately, the gas infrastructure is not given enough space in the report. we need to put more emphasis on regional cooperation. in this context, appendix iv to the vidal quadras report can help us, which we have already adopted on the question of gas security.
the modernisation of european development policy must necessarily be based on an evaluation of the way in which european union development policy has operated in the past. i am convinced that the european union must do much more to promote the working and business habits of the people of developing countries, so that they gradually move from primitive, inefficient gainful activities, or sometimes from idleness due to the lack of job opportunities, to work that is necessary for society and that also provides a decent adequate income to those who carry it out. at the same time, it is necessary to ensure that business rules in these countries are simple and tax systems are simple and fair. we must strive to teach the citizens of these countries, as they say, to fish, not to give them fish.

the production of genetically modified food is a highly sensitive issue and one that is closely watched by the general public. the acceptance of genetically modified products in the food chain varies from one country to another and therefore the right of each country to decide for itself and to restrict the prohibition of gmos on its territory is fully legitimate. the principles defining the rules under which individual member states may restrict or prohibit the production of gmos on their territory, contained in mrs lepage's report, are a step forward in the search for a truly responsible way of deciding on this issue. indeed, to leave the right to authorise gmos at a central european level solely for the sake of protecting the single european market is, in my view, unsustainable. the commercial interests of producers must be responsibly directed and regulated so that our citizens do not lose confidence in our food policy.
the current cross-border cooperation in enforcing consumer protection legislation, and that is the key word, is unfortunately very frustrating, unattainable, rather abstract for many european citizens. the need to establish a genuinely effective legal enforcement mechanism would therefore clearly lead to an increase in european consumers' confidence in the internal market and, consequently, to a revival of cross-border trade. businesses, consumers and enforcement authorities need a clear legal framework and thus legal certainty in the cross-border enforcement of the consumer acquis. for this reason, i fully agree that cross-border enforcement of consumer interests should be incorporated at the forefront of the political agenda of the european union.
we voted on a directive which gives member states the possibility of restricting or banning genetically modified organisms. there are possible cumulative long-term effects, both direct and indirect, effects on human health, but also on the environment. as we know, there are three main reasons, three categories, when we evaluate genetically modified organisms. these are: environmental issues, but also issues of resistance to pesticides; secondly, there are socio-economic reasons, because we have the cost of decontamination; and then there is land planning and land management as such. safety risks must be assessed, as well as the rules for coexistence of different varieties. i am against such waste of land in the controversial effort to plant gmo organisms on large areas to produce so-called green diesel for motor vehicles. on the other hand, such practices directly raise the price of other foods and do not contribute much to the environment. and by the way, most citizens are against the planting of gmos in our soil, and i would rely on the european food safety agency to give expert opinions on this.

the current threshold for receiving aid between the convergence and competitiveness objectives is clearly set at 75% of community gdp. i fully agree with the rapporteur that a new general category based on funding and based on gdp at 75% to 90% is contrary to the key philosophy of eu cohesion policy, which is to support the weakest regions through a horizontal approach. the introduction of a new category of regions does not entail any increase in resources, which could mean that the convergence regions with the most structural, economic and social problems would have to be reduced after 2013 in favour of the more developed regions, which would no longer be covered by the convergence objective according to the current criteria. this would negatively affect up to 50 regions with 72 million citizens and inequalities between regions could persist.

in writing. − the single air transport market in the european union has been legislated in such a way that the application of the rights established in air transport is primarily for the benefit of passengers. lower prices are available and more carriers are available than ever before. the eu has also taken steps to improve air safety, drawing up a list of airlines that have not proved safe and are banned or restricted within the union. it provides passengers with special rights in the event of their flights being disrupted in any way (delayed, cancelled) or multiple tickets being sold for one place. eu legislation assumes responsibility for loss, delay or damage to baggage. new rules have also been created to protect disabled persons and persons with reduced mobility from discrimination and to ensure that they receive the necessary assistance during the flight. for example, these legislative measures were also taken by the eu in an effort to ensure the fair treatment of air passengers.

in writing. − in june 2009, the commission presented two legislative initiatives to establish an agency to manage large-scale information systems within the area of freedom, security and justice. the first initiative was a draft regulation on first pillar issues relating to sis, vis and eurodac, the second a draft decision on third pillar issues relating to these systems. however, with the entry into force of the treaty of lisbon, these initiatives have become irrelevant, since, although the three pillars have been avoided, the proposal in question bears the hallmarks of a variable geometry, which is reflected in the various aspects of the area of freedom, security and justice in general and in the schengen area in particular. the legal framework of the schemes to be managed by the agency covers a diverse group of member states with different levels of participation (as regards the united kingdom, denmark and ireland) and associated third countries (norway, iceland, switzerland and, in the future, liechtenstein). the commission has carried out an impact assessment to determine what would be the best solution from a financial, operational and institutional perspective. the creation of a european agency seems to be the most appropriate solution, but it is important to stress that the objectives and tasks of the agency relate exclusively to the technical level of operational management. the agency shall not have the power to take political decisions, for example to establish new systems or to take decisions on the interoperability of systems.
in writing. − article 349 of the treaty on the functioning of the european union authorises the european council, on a proposal from the commission and after consulting the european parliament, to adopt measures in favour of the outermost regions, taking account of their economic and social situation. the existence of permanent handicaps such as insularity, great distance from major markets, small size, terrain, difficult climate and economic dependence on a small number of products seriously hampers the development of these regions and fully justifies the application of appropriate measures. this is the basis for the system which allows france to apply a different rate of tax called 'octroi de mer' in the four french overseas departments until 1 july 2014 to certain products produced in the overseas departments. this system is essential for the stability of the economies of the relevant outermost regions, as it allows the preservation of local production and employment. similarly, the revenues from the 'octroi de mer' allocated to the regions play an important role in supporting investment policies aimed at local development. i therefore believe that the exemption or reduction of the 'octroi de mer' granted to the french overseas departments should be maintained, and that it would be appropriate to consider maintaining those measures definitively, in order to avoid creating a situation of economic uncertainty in the outermost regions concerned every ten years.

in writing. − the threat posed to humanity by climate change is not diminishing, and global warming of 2°c is having an even more serious impact than originally thought. although extreme weather events cannot be clearly attributed to global warming, climate change is likely to increase the frequency and intensity of such events. however, the fact that the international community has failed to reach a comprehensive, binding international climate treaty in copenhagen does not mean that countries are not taking action. because european countries face crucial decisions to preserve their future prosperity and security. we can link the transition to an eu-wide greenhouse gas emissions reduction target that is in line with the eu's climate goals with a healthier economy, growth in green jobs and innovation. without significant reductions in the emission ceilings, the eu emissions trading system risks becoming unnecessary in stimulating investment in green technologies and innovation. it is therefore essential to make the necessary efforts to reduce greenhouse gas emissions. because the benefits for european citizens would also be increased by improving air quality in europe and stimulating investment in the eu economy.
in writing. − european countries must make critical choices now if they are to safeguard their future prosperity and security. a move towards a national greenhouse gas emission reduction target that is also consistent with eu climate change objectives is needed. here, a healthier economy, more green jobs and more innovation should play the biggest role. in 2009, the european union already achieved 17.3% of its commitment to reduce co2 emissions by 20% in the europe 2020 strategy. a lot of people think that by 2020, we can change that commitment and maybe even increase it to 25 percent. however, i do not share this view, especially in view of the changes in eu nuclear energy policy since fukushima. it should be borne in mind that our initial proposals are based on an energy mix in which nuclear energy is an integral part of the programmes of several countries. if that changes, the overall 25% will be difficult to meet. in view of the above, i think it is important that our member states do not completely shut themselves off from the possibilities of zero-carbon nuclear energy. on the basis of the above, i did not vote for the amendments which aimed at the 25% increase, but i supported the report as a whole.
in writing. - cohesion policy is something without which the european union as we know it and want to know it would not exist. but this report does not quite understand cohesion. the report warns of the threat of the eu losing its demographic and economic importance by 2050. in the light of this 'threat', it concludes that 'if the european community of states is to assert itself in economic and political competition and if this relative loss of importance is not to be accompanied by a decline in the level of welfare, the community must stand together more strongly on important issues of future security'. i do not think that the community should stick together for these reasons the purpose of cohesion policy should not be to maintain the eu's global economic positions and compete with the rest of the world. the aim should be to build cohesion between nations and to build citizens' sense of identity with the eu. so that europeans can feel equal in their own country and in the eu. the eu's cohesion policy is a unique policy approach on a global scale which i believe needs to be promoted.
in writing. − budget support means the transfer of funds from an external financing agency to the national budget of a partner country, if that country fulfils the conditions for making a payment. the funds thus obtained shall form part of the partner country's overall resources and shall therefore be used in accordance with the partner country's public finance management system. although budget support has been granted for a longer period, this practice became widespread in the 1980s and 1990s, when the world bank and various bilateral cooperation groups began to provide budget support in the form of balance of payments assistance. the second wave of budget support introduced a new coordinated approach to general budget support in the period 2000-05. the aim of this form of budget support was to bring support to partner countries' policies and strategies, to develop concepts of accountability and enhanced partnership, to better harmonise procedures, modalities and disbursements of support between aid providers. however, in order to be eligible, countries must achieve a sufficient level of responsibility in the areas of poverty reduction, macroeconomic governance, public finance management and governance.
in writing. − the lisbon treaty has as a fundamental objective to promote the interconnection of energy networks. progress within the eu has not been easy, and there are many areas of friction between countries in energy policy, many national interests in the way, and fragmented markets. all obstacles can only be overcome with determination and energy policy. both of these elements are part of the energy 2020 communication, which calls for a radical change in the approach to be taken to extremely important issues such as energy infrastructure and networks, to be mobilised and supported in the name of a 'resource efficient europe'. i believe that the energy structures that are of particular importance to the eu's decades-long ambitions should be the focus of attention, namely the reduction of carbon, the guarantee of security of supply and price stability for consumers, and the creation of a single energy market that ensures access to affordable energy sources for businesses and citizens. solidarity between member states is also important in this respect, and it is impossible to speak of security without also mentioning solidarity within europe. it is time for europe to act as one and to set common short, medium and long-term energy policy objectives for the benefit of european citizens and businesses.

in writing. − if you have in accordance with the convention implementing the schengen agreement of 14 june 1985, the guide to travel documents entitling the holder to cross the external borders and bearing a visa has been adapted. however, these decisions cover the period of schengen cooperation at intergovernmental level and need to be adapted to the current eu institutional and legal framework. the purpose of the list of travel documents is twofold: on the one hand, it allows border control to verify whether a certain travel document has been recognised for the purpose of crossing the external borders, and on the other hand, it allows consular staff to verify whether member states recognise a certain travel document for the purpose of affixing a visa sticker. in this context, a measure seems necessary to ensure that the list of travel documents is kept up to date and that the fullest possible information is made available to the member states. in the interests of simplicity and efficiency, member states would be required to communicate their opinion on the recognition or non-recognition of those documents. the proposal as such should therefore represent an added value as one of the union acts, by offering certainty to the border guards who have the right to check travel documents at the external borders. the list of travel documents should therefore be legally binding, as well as being consistent with the competence of member states to recognise travel documents.
in writing. − by 2020, all europeans should have access to internet speeds of more than 30 megabits per second (mbps) and at least 50% of households in europe should have internet speeds of more than 100 mbps. this objective is part of the digital agenda for europe, the priority initiative of the europe 2020 strategy aimed at a smart, sustainable and inclusive economy. the digital agenda also confirmed the european council's objective of providing basic broadband to all europeans by 2013. to achieve these ambitious goals, a comprehensive policy based on the full range of technologies needs to be developed and progress made closely monitored. the objective of providing a fast and ultra-fast internet was highlighted because it will play a central role in the economic recovery and will be a platform to promote innovation throughout the economy, as was the case with electricity and transport in the past. the deployment of ultra-fast open and competitive networks will stimulate a positive cycle in the development of the digital economy, as it will allow the emergence and expansion of new services requiring broadband and for which citizens' demand will increase, resulting in increased broadband demand.
in writing. − the world around us has changed radically, thanks to rapid technological developments and globalisation, and new challenges have emerged in the area of personal data protection. technology today allows individuals to share information about their behaviour and preferences and, on an unprecedented scale, to make it public and globally available. social networking sites, with hundreds of millions of members scattered around the world, are among the most prominent. a recent study confirmed that data protection authorities, business associations and consumer organisations agree that online activities pose increased risks to privacy and personal data protection. at the same time, the ways in which personal data is collected are becoming more complex and more difficult to detect. the question is therefore whether existing eu data protection legislation can still respond fully and effectively to potential threats. despite the existence of a common eu legal framework on data protection, one of the main concerns of stakeholders is the lack of harmonisation of member states' legislation. i believe that it is desirable for the eu to develop a comprehensive and coherent approach to ensure that the fundamental right of individuals to data protection is fully respected, both within and outside the eu.
in writing. − nutrition labelling the following information is required for the labelling of the product: the recent white paper on a strategy to tackle health problems related to nutrition, overweight and obesity in europe highlighted the need for consumers to have access to clear, consistent and proven information. nutrition labelling is an established means of providing information to consumers to promote health-conscious food choices. there is a broad consensus that the effectiveness of nutrition labelling can be enhanced as a means of promoting consumers' ability to choose a balanced diet. several suggestions were made by interested parties in support of the inclusion of nutrition information on the front of packages. the labelling systems used differ in what may create barriers to trade. the proposal introduces certain general principles concerning the provision of food information and develops a management mechanism in the light of developments to enable consumers to make informed food choices. the mandatory requirements remain broadly the same, but the commission has the possibility to propose new requirements for specific issues. in order to take account of changes and developments in the field of food information, it is necessary to lay down provisions to empower the commission to amend the list of mandatory information by adding or removing data and to make certain data available by alternative means. consultation with stakeholders should allow for timely and well-targeted changes to food information requirements.
in writing. − the 2001 white paper on european transport policy sets an ambitious european union target of halving the number of road fatalities by 2010. and despite the declining number of road fatalities, the target set in the white paper is unfortunately not being achieved. the proposal was based on studies which showed that the proportion of accidents involving drivers in a non-resident country is disproportionately high, mainly due to speeding. penalties for offences committed in the territory of member states where drivers are not resident are generally not enforced, in particular for automatically registered offences. this relative impunity undermines the objectives set in the field of road safety and weakens the legality of these checks in the eyes of european citizens who might question them, given the need for equal access to all, regardless of whether they are resident in the country concerned. the commission aims to facilitate the enforcement of penalties for drivers who have committed offences of speeding, driving under the influence of alcohol, not wearing seatbelts or failing to stop at a red light in a foreign member state. the commission has deliberately decided to limit the scope of the directive to these four offences, which are the cause of the highest number of fatal accidents and are regarded as offences in all the member states of the european union.

in writing. − tses are a group of diseases occurring in both humans and animals and are characterised by degeneration of brain tissue that takes on a sponge-like appearance and eventually causes death. in response to the bse epidemic in the eu, a regulation of the european parliament and of the council laying down rules for the prevention, control and eradication of certain spongiform encephalopathies (known as the tse regulation) was adopted. the regulation established for the first time a single legal basis for the control and prevention of tses and bse. that regulation consolidated all the transitional eu legislation in the field of tses. it has been amended several times since its introduction and certain additional measures have been amended with a view to further eradicating, controlling and monitoring tses. in addition, other measures contribute to the comprehensive safety and monitoring regime governing tses. i consider it essential that consumer protection, animal health and the eradication of tses should always be the main objectives and be of primary importance when considering possible changes to the applicable rules, and that the evolution of the tse group of diseases should continue to be closely monitored in the event of a recurrence of tses/bses. it is also necessary to strengthen research in those areas where knowledge is still incomplete. only in this way can reasoned policy decisions be taken in the future.

the european parliament is a key element of the constitutional order of the european union. in addition to the lengthy negotiations on the revision of the treaty, the union has made substantial progress in creating the basic conditions for uniform elections, despite the lack of a uniform electoral law. as regards the problems encountered by previous rapporteurs, some were successfully resolved. there is a category of issues that may have seemed problematic at the beginning of the process of introducing direct elections, but as my predecessor said, we need to focus on progress, and therefore many of them have already been resolved. the importance and powers of parliament have grown considerably since 1979, including the treaty of lisbon, which considerably extended our powers. parliament therefore needs and deserves a new electoral system and internal organisation that correspond to its new tasks. last but not least, it is also about making the elections to the european parliament easier, more understandable and more attractive for the citizens of the member states.
since its inception, the european union has been developing and changing dynamically. with its enlargement, the mechanisms for representing the citizens of the member states in the political bodies of the union must also be revised. it is therefore right that we are already dealing with the reform of the 2014 european elections. mr duff's report makes a number of proposals for amendments which are acceptable. however, pragmatic changes are eluding the proposal to create 25 additional mandates for parliament elected on a separate pan-european ticket. i agree with mr duff that the body of the european parliament could be divided into two separate chambers. the chamber of union citizens, created under the current rules, would be based in brussels and would carry out the current tasks of parliament. a chamber of state representatives, with not 25, but x times as many seats as there are in the union of states, say 3 times 27 today, would be based in strasbourg and would act as a mediator and coordinator in disputes between the supreme institutions of the european union. the chamber of representatives of states could also act as a brake on the majoritarianism of small states in the majority decision-making of the chamber of citizens of the union. such a change could be beneficial.

in writing. − article 9 of protocol (no 1) provides that the organisation and promotion of effective and regular interparliamentary cooperation must be defined jointly by the european parliament and the national parliaments. the european parliament shall co-decide with the council on the eu budget for external action, including the budget for civilian missions under the cfsp and the csdp and for administrative costs related to eu military coordination. in accordance with the treaty, the european parliament is regularly consulted on the main aspects and basic options of the cfsp and its consent is essential for the transformation of eu strategies into legislation and for the conclusion of international agreements, including those relating mainly to the cfsp. it is clear that the european parliament is a source of democratic legitimacy in the areas of the cfsp and the csdp over which it exercises political control. i am also convinced that strengthening interparliamentary cooperation in the cfsp and csdp will enhance parliamentary influence on the political decisions of the eu and its states, given the european parliament's responsibility for the common policies of the union, including the cfsp/csdp, and the prerogatives of all national parliaments in deciding on security and defence policy at national level. parliament should be represented in any new form of interparliamentary cooperation to an extent that reflects the scope and importance of its role in the control of the cfsp/cfsp, recognises the common european nature of those policies and meets the need to express its political and geographical pluralism.
in writing. − approximately 43 million people in the european union are at risk of food shortages and it is estimated that the economic and financial crisis, as well as the sharp rise in prices, are putting more and more people at risk of food shortages. some 80 million people in the union are at risk of poverty and the crisis could increase this number. the eu's food for the most deprived programme, established in 1987 under the common agricultural policy, currently provides food aid to 13 million people affected by poverty in 19 member states and includes a distribution chain of 240 food banks and charities. it is undeniable that the abrupt termination of an existing and functioning aid programme without prior notification or preparation would have a significant impact on the most vulnerable eu citizens. however, as the eu intervention stocks have been significantly reduced, a solution to the current stalemate on this issue needs to be found at council level, and also the most appropriate legal basis for the next financial planning period. the right to food is one of the fundamental human rights and can only be ensured if all people have continuous physical, social and economically sustainable access to adequate, safe and nutritious food that meets their nutritional needs and priorities for an active and healthy life.
in writing. − the european parliament, elected by direct universal suffrage, is a key element of the constitutional order of the european union. in addition to the lengthy negotiations on the revision of the eu treaty, substantial progress has been made in creating the basic conditions for uniform elections to the european parliament, despite the lack of a uniform electoral law. as regards the problems encountered by previous rapporteurs on this issue, some have been successfully resolved. there is another category of issues that might have seemed problematic at the beginning of the process of introducing direct elections, but that experience has made less so. these include the eligibility of independent candidates and the control of electoral expenditure. parliament's importance and powers have grown considerably since 1979. the treaty of lisbon, which finally came into force, also considerably extended the powers of meps. parliament therefore needs and deserves an electoral system and internal organisation that are appropriate to its new tasks. it is clear that a large number of important electoral issues remain, which, if effectively resolved, would contribute to making the next parliamentary elections more uniform than in the past and should be beneficial in terms of coherence, legitimacy, efficiency and pluralism. perhaps it is time to think more seriously about finding a mathematical formula for the redistribution of seats that is durable, transparent and politically neutral.
in writing. − the european union has been actively involved in mine action, particularly since the 1995 joint action, and has adopted the binding objective of completely banning and eliminating anti-personnel landmines worldwide. it is a leading promoter and contributor to mine action, and this theme is one of its priorities in the areas of human rights, humanitarian and development aid. mine action includes the search, detection, marking and disposal of anti-personnel landmines and other explosive remnants of war, including abandoned arsenal, unexploded ordnance, remnants of cluster munitions and improvised explosive devices, as well as mine risk education, assistance to victims, stockpile disposal and support to promote the general extension of relevant international conventions and treaties to end the production, use and trafficking of anti-personnel landmines. in addition to causing loss of life, especially among the civilian population, they represent a serious obstacle to the post-conflict reconstruction of the affected countries and can serve as a raw material for the manufacture of improvised explosive devices. it is gratifying to note that 156 countries have already signed and ratified the mine ban treaty, including 25 eu member states.

for the efd group mr president, commissioner, as mr bütikofer's report shows, european industry is finding it increasingly difficult to obtain the raw materials needed for innovative production. the strong industrial growth in third world countries, especially in asia and south america, is increasing the demand for raw materials, precious metals or rare earth elements, driving up their prices and making them less available to european industry. however, europe has long been a major source of waste, often containing rare metals or hard-to-find materials from abroad. so, in addition to looking for new sources of raw materials, whether through trade diplomacy or cooperation in the discovery of new mining capacities, i think we need to focus more on exploiting the potential of waste recycling. indeed, recyclable industrial waste should no longer be considered as just worthless pollution. on the contrary, it is a potential new source of raw materials that will make it possible to reduce, at least in part, the european union's dependence on countries supplying its missing raw materials.

in writing − if you have in most industrialized countries, including all eu member states and emerging economies, there is at least one state-supported export credit agency. these agencies represent the most important source of public financial support for projects in the private sector. the amount of support they provide for large industrial and infrastructure projects in developing countries is several times higher than the total annual allocations of all multilateral development banks. they facilitate legitimate trade in the event that the private capital market fails. they have a much higher risk-taking capacity than private entities, since they do not have to pay taxes and generate profits, and are therefore more protected than private banks in the event of interest-bearing loan settlement. however, for the same reason, they can also be a major trade disturbance if their financial operations are not governed by common rules. export credit agencies are public policy instruments that are well placed to contribute to the financing of the international objectives to which the eu is committed. the entry into force of the treaty of lisbon requires a strengthening of coherence across the eu's external action. export credit agencies must also be assessed against these objectives. i think it is appropriate to include in the agreement on state-supported export credit those requirements which could lead these agencies in the eu member states to contribute to eu policies and objectives.

written. − european industry is facing an increasingly difficult situation in terms of raw material supply. the eu is highly dependent on imports for many raw materials. moreover, the lack of resources can exacerbate the situation on the international political scene and, if necessary, lead to a struggle for resources and to a widening of the gap between resource-rich and resource-poor countries. therefore, new approaches addressing non-energy, non-agricultural raw materials need to be developed to ultimately avoid situations where one party always wins and the other always loses. in addition to the industrial innovation strategy aimed at reducing resource consumption and increasing recycling, the european union will continue to rely on external suppliers for raw materials. raw materials diplomacy is therefore essential. in this context, the european union needs to forge mutually beneficial partnerships that benefit both resource-rich countries and the eu itself. in order to successfully address the raw materials problem, the union needs a comprehensive and integrated strategy focusing on short-term and long-term measures that can be implemented both domestically and abroad, in particular with regard to critical raw materials. i believe that it is essential to seek to ensure future competitiveness, sustainability and security of supply through appropriate measures.
written − the rapporteur points to the importance of diplomacy in gaining access to strategic minerals (such as metals used in technological sectors) for european industry; he considers this to be one of the tasks of the european external action service. it also points to opportunities in the eu that could reduce imports from third countries: own extraction and production (including research and development of new technologies), but also recycling, reuse and recovery of raw materials and metals from landfills. the eu's mineral strategy must be effective and fair; it must also respect the right of developing countries to benefit from their own mineral resources. the objectives of the strategy are to further develop european industry, increase recycling rates and make the management of natural resources more efficient across the eu.

the fundamental right of access to documents of the institutions, bodies, offices and agencies of the european union is unquestionable. transparency must be the foundation of any participatory democracy and should ideally complement representative democracy. the treaty on european union allows citizens to participate in the decision-making process and thus exercise public control, thereby guaranteeing the legitimacy of the democratic political system. the commission proposed in 2008 an update of the regulation on public access to parliament, council and commission documents. however, the amendments proposed by the commission do not improve the level of access to documents of the institutions. the inappropriate definition of what constitutes a document limits the scope of the data available and is therefore contrary to the treaty of lisbon. i would therefore ask the commission to revise its proposals and i am also convinced that steps can be taken in the legislative process. the public could thus be much better informed if the parliamentary committees adopted indicative votes before the negotiations and the council published the negotiating positions agreed within coreper.

for the efd group the phenomenon of homelessness has long been a drag on europe's civilised and cultural society. street homelessness is the most visible and extreme form of poverty and social exclusion. the reasons for this situation vary. often, these are personal factors, such as a break-up in a relationship, domestic violence, the death of a partner, loss of employment, illegal immigration, substance abuse, or the complete loss of earning potential. the european consensus conference on homelessness last december sought to answer the question of how to deal with this unpleasant phenomenon that frustrates all decent people. the basic and first measure should be prevention by minimising the threat of eviction in cases of personal problems. the commission should also be able to provide the necessary information to the member states in order to enable them to take appropriate measures to ensure that the emergency accommodation is provided in a timely manner. consequently, after overcoming the worst problems, the disabled should be able to work their way to cheap, simple but stable accommodation by their own best efforts. of course, other assistance will have to be provided for the homeless in addition to housing. however, this should also be granted primarily for their active cooperation.
in december, i joined more than half of my colleagues in calling on the commission to adopt an effective and comprehensive union strategy to combat street homelessness. we are therefore now asking the commission what has actually happened since then, what measures have you taken and we would also like to know whether you would like to work with us on such a strategy. a strategy to combat street homelessness should include several elements. it should have a clear and measurable objective, it should be cross-cutting across all relevant policies. it should have a clear dimension in housing policy and should also take into account changes in the character of the population, whether it concerns, for example, the effects of immigration, but also the ever-deepening poverty as a result of the economic and social crisis also in the member states of the european union. reporting on strategies to combat homelessness should be included in the national strategic reports submitted under the open method of coordination in the social field. i would therefore like to call on the commission once again to ensure that effective measures are implemented and to work with us on a concrete strategy to combat street homelessness.
homelessness is one of the most extreme and worst manifestations of poverty and social exclusion. homeless people are found every day outside shopping malls, in the basements, on the streets, neglected, dirty, hungry. solidarity is a hallmark of the european union. awareness that all people have the right to a life of dignity, an understanding that society as a whole benefits from the eradication of poverty, must engage all layers of society to eradicate this phenomenon. i see a space here for individuals, both public and private. the awareness campaigns that are being prepared should help to do this, but the time has come for us to bring in a pan-european system of cooperation between the member states.
all people can find themselves in a very difficult situation without a roof over their heads. a number of problems, such as work, financial, family, or psychological difficulties, pile up, plunging such a person into a hopeless situation. the joint efforts of local and regional authorities and the european institutions thus become a necessary prerequisite for creating a lasting solution to this problem. structural funds directed towards housing strategies for socially disadvantaged groups should also be explicitly earmarked for addressing the problems of homelessness and their specific use must be monitored and evaluated accordingly. in conclusion, i would like to express my conviction that homelessness is incompatible with the values of a modern inclusive society and the european union, and therefore i appreciate that the strategy 2020, whose main objective is to save at least 20 million people from the threat of poverty and social exclusion by 2020, has given room to address the issue of homelessness as well.
let me give you a look that hasn't been seen before. if the family works, homelessness is a marginal phenomenon. we need to help people who have lost everything and can't help themselves anymore. but this parliament still passes a lot of legislation that weakens the family. the commission and parliament are doing everything possible to ensure that mothers entrust the care of their children to strangers in collective institutions as soon as possible. it's at the expense of building relationships. we talk about reconciling work and family life, but we refuse to recognize the value of a woman's work, who takes care of children, close relatives, or the home. when a person is on the street, we draft resolutions, we call committees, we commission studies, and we devise strategies. but what we fail to realize is that building and maintaining a home takes effort, time, and energy. it's a tough job. if no one does it, the family and the home will perish. some people manage to save their roof over their heads, but some don't.
the european union is doing a lot to improve the climate gradually. it is a leader in designing and promoting effective measures to reduce carbon dioxide emissions across the global community. however, current evidence suggests that a more comprehensive approach to anthropogenic emissions will be needed to save the climate. it appears that, as the question put forward suggests, we should gradually start to reduce the production and consumption of hydrofluorocarbons, to reduce black carbon emissions or to limit the production of gases contributing to tropospheric ozone. already, the montreal protocol can be relied upon in expanding efforts to reduce the production and consumption of hydrofluorocarbons at international level immediately. but experience of the world community's current behaviour shows us that even further measures needed to improve the climate will need to be prepared and initiated again here in europe. but the sooner we start doing that, the sooner other countries around the world can join our efforts to improve the climate.

approximately 10 years after the gradual liberalisation of the electricity and natural gas markets, it is clear that the energy exchanges that have emerged and the otc trading contracts that have become virtually ubiquitous have never been protected against attempts to manipulate markets and trade using inside information. the liberalisation of energy markets was highlighted as a necessary measure to reduce the cost of electricity and gas to consumers. in fact, prices tended to rise and energy poverty became a concomitant phenomenon in the ongoing liberalisation. the proposed specific regulation of energy markets recognises the specific nature of these markets, while proposing that it be subject to the rules on market abuse and insider dealing applicable to financial markets. that is why i supported this proposal for a regulation.
the energy market integrity and transparency regulation provides a union legal framework to prevent market abuse and manipulation in the wholesale energy market. the objective of the liberalisation introduced was to create the conditions for the internal market by 2014. however, liberalisation has not achieved its objective, energy prices have not been uniformised, prices have increased and their volatility has increased. i believe that by screening out unfair practices we can achieve a stabilisation and uniformity of energy market prices, and thus put our end-users in a better position than they are today. however, wholesale contracts are easily bought and resold and are therefore more exposed to market manipulation. that is why we need more effective market surveillance. on the basis of the national registers, a union register of operators should be established, to which the relevant authorities should also have access. that is why i voted in favour of this proposal.
i supported the report, but let me highlight one important fact. the treaty of lisbon gave more powers to national parliaments. this subsidiarity element needs to be used more effectively. i therefore join in assessing the nature of this cooperation. if it proves to be ineffective, it should be reviewed. in particular, it is necessary to adapt the current time limits in order to allow national parliaments to exercise their right to express an opinion or to object to a breach of the principle of subsidiarity. because the opposite of subsidiarity is centralization, and the result of centralization is the loss of real democracy, of people's influence in solving problems that directly concern them. the principle of subsidiarity was also partly contradicted by our discussion this morning on the financial crisis and the future of the euro. many of our colleagues, including the president of the european commission, have been in favour of community decision-making at the expense of the european council.

in writing − unfair practices in wholesale energy markets affect price levels so that they cannot fulfil their role of sending a clear signal to power plants, households and businesses on the optimal use of energy, providing guidance for sound investment in energy infrastructure and promoting energy efficiency. instead, such practices may cause high price volatility, lead to higher energy prices for final consumers and undermine the confidence of potential investors in energy infrastructure projects. the transparency of energy markets is a necessary prerequisite for further integration of the eu energy market, which is expected to bring important benefits to consumers. the remit regulation therefore acts as a key instrument to achieve the objective set by the european council of completing the internal market by 2014. in order to avoid further liberalisation of energy markets, this regulation should not apply to very small market participants and therefore to transactions below a certain volume. this will avoid new market entrants facing an excessive burden when entering energy markets. market participants trading below a certain threshold should not be required to notify their transactions or be subject to licensing requirements (de minimis rule). the regulation should improve transparency, integrity and stability in the wholesale energy market. citizens have the right to know how and with what results public funds are allocated and spent. it is therefore necessary for the eu institutions to apply this principle in relation to the running of the institution and the policies and the financial resources allocated to their implementation at all levels.

in writing − the report focuses on the commission's essential role as guardian of the treaty and on the commission's power and duty to initiate infringement proceedings against a member state which has failed to fulfil an obligation under the treaty. the infringement procedure consists of two stages: the administrative (investigation) stage and the judicial stage before the court of justice. in the administrative phase, citizens (complainants) have a key role to play in ensuring compliance with union law on the ground. bringing europe closer to its citizens and embracing good governance are essentially interlinked areas. one area of direct interaction between europe and eu citizens is precisely the administrative phase of article 258 tfeu, in which citizens turn to the commission and parliament for assistance in accessing their european rights. it is therefore of the utmost importance that complainants are treated in accordance with the principles of good administration. the commission should propose 'procedural legislation' in the form of a regulation under the new legal basis of article 298 tfeu in order to strengthen citizens' rights and guarantee transparency.
written − the treaty of lisbon, which entered into force on 1 december 2009, introduced a number of new legal bases to facilitate the implementation and enforcement of eu law, significantly changing the legal and regulatory environment at european level. in the european union, as in any democratic and legal state, individual measures must be specific, in accordance with the applicable legal norms and at the same time in accordance with the principle of predictability and the objective correctness of decisions, so that eu citizens and all economic actors can enjoy their rights under the legislation with confidence and effectively. it is therefore of the utmost importance that eu legislation is as transparent, understandable and accessible as possible. i believe that a considerable effort needs to be made in the area of transparency and the strengthening of good governance at european level, which remains very remote and inaccessible to the ordinary citizen of the eu. i therefore support and vote in favour of the recommendations set out in the annual report on the monitoring of the application of eu law and the call to the commission to propose new legislation to strengthen citizens' rights and guarantee transparency.
in writing − the lisbon agreement established a new constitutional framework for eu institutional transparency in the interests of an open, efficient and independent european administration by establishing an unwavering fundamental right of access to documents of the eu institutions, bodies, offices and agencies. the treaty confers this right not only on eu citizens but also on any natural or legal person residing in a member state, and it should be applied in accordance with the general principles and limits (established with a view to protecting certain public or private interests) laid down in the rules adopted by the european parliament and the council. the general rule currently applies that access to legislative documents should be fully guaranteed, while the exceptions for non-legislative documents should be narrowed and the two approaches should not interfere with each other. transparency is an essential part of participatory democracy and complements the representative democracy on which the functioning of the eu is based, as expressly stated in articles 9 to 11 teu, allowing citizens to participate in the decision-making process and exercise public scrutiny, thus guaranteeing the legitimacy of the democratic political system. similarly, common rules for the classification of documents must be based on legislation. i also express my full support for free thinking within the bodies and the institution, and for the appropriate balance between transparency and data protection.

written − the european union entered a new phase with the adoption of the treaty of lisbon, which directly established a new constitutional framework for eu institutional transparency with a view to creating an open, efficient and independent european administration. by establishing an unwavering fundamental right of access to documents of the eu institutions, bodies, offices and agencies, participatory democracy enabling citizens to participate in the decision-making process, exercise public scrutiny and thus guarantee the legitimacy of the democratic political system becomes a reality. citizens can directly participate in the democratic process, control how public funds are spent and also directly fight corruption, which is linked precisely to the opacity of mechanisms and the closure of institutions. however, the reality of everyday life remains more mundane, and for the reasons mentioned above, i fully support the demands made in the access to documents report that all eu institutions, bodies, offices and agencies act proactively and make available to the public on their websites, in addition to general activity documents, budgets and lists of closed public procurement contracts. in particular, i would like to stress the strong need to ensure transparency in the management of european funds, where it seems necessary to systematically publish the same categories of information on all beneficiaries of the european funds on a single website. such action will clearly strengthen citizens' confidence in the european union's actions and the sound management of its funds.

written − with the entry into force of the treaty of lisbon on 1 december 2009, the charter of fundamental rights became legally binding. as regards petitions received, fundamental rights are the second most frequent topic in petitions submitted. the incorporation of the charter into eu primary law on the basis of the principle of subsidiarity means that member states are responsible for respecting the principles of the charter of fundamental rights. this has created new responsibilities for the decision-making and executive institutions, as well as for the member states, in the application of eu law at national level. the provisions of the charter thus became directly enforceable by both european and national courts.

in writing − when the eu decided to reduce greenhouse gas emissions in 2008, it showed its commitment to combating the threat of climate change and set an example to the world by showing how this problem could be tackled. the agreement to reduce emissions by 20% by 2020 compared to 1990 levels, together with the achievement of 20% renewable energy, was a key step for the eu's sustainable development and a clear signal to the rest of the world that the union was ready to take the necessary action. but these alone are not enough to meet the target of keeping global warming below 2°c compared to pre-industrial levels. at the same time, the eu economy has come under severe pressure from the crisis. businesses today are under pressure from falling demand and the challenge of finding sources of finance. by reducing the price of carbon emissions, the revenue to the national treasury from emissions trading could also be halved, thus increasing the pressure on public finances and limiting the potential additional source of public funds that could be used to combat climate change. the need to find the investments needed to achieve the 20% target for renewable energy in areas such as electricity, heating and transport remains.
in writing. − the objective of limiting the global annual average surface temperature increase to 2 oc (the so-called 2 oc target) has become an international goal since the cancún agreements. failure to meet this target will have huge environmental consequences and enormous economic costs and will increase the likelihood of reaching an endpoint where temperature levels begin to affect the release of co2 and ch4 from storage sites such as forests and permafrost and limit nature's ability to absorb carbon in the oceans. european climate policy must take into account all sources of warming and all mitigation options. the european commission must inform the european parliament of any action it takes in this area.

corruption is a serious problem in a modern democratic society. although the union has made great efforts to develop measures and legislation to combat this adverse phenomenon, several member states are still delaying its implementation. at a time when representatives of the fair play alliance are also confirming that european anti-corruption legislation meets the necessary parameters, it is important to make some more efforts to enforce its application. we therefore need to focus more on monitoring mechanisms by independent experts or civil society organisations to contribute to the detection of suspected corruption and to the better use of existing regulations. we should also seek to speed up investigations or better protect whistleblowers. it would also be good to harmonise sanctions for corruption of foreign nationals across the union. i am convinced that only by calm, patient and systematic work can we succeed in this endeavor.

in writing. corruption is one of the international threats that pose a challenge to the internal security of the union. the consequences of corruption often reach across or beyond the eu's borders. four out of five eu citizens consider corruption a serious problem in their country. corruption costs us €120 billion a year, or 1% of the european union's gdp. it undermines the rule of law, distorts the market and has contributed to the current economic crisis. all eu institutions, including eu agencies, as well as member states, should ensure greater transparency. the commission and eurojust should ensure a more efficient and faster exchange of documents and information between national courts in cases of corruption with a cross-border dimension. the commission shall ensure the political coordination of the anti-corruption mechanism.

floods are among the most devastating natural events in terms of loss of life and property. the least developed countries are the most vulnerable to climate change and inadequate flood control. it is therefore important to adopt a multi-level flood strategy, especially in regions where unstable glacial lakes pose a critical flood threat. i agree with my fellow rapporteur who warns against relying on large dams to prevent flood damage, especially in the context of climate change. extreme rainfall is likely to increase the intensity and frequency of flash floods, which may reduce the safety level of dams. the commission notes that the project is not a 'competitive' project, but a 'competitive' project. in economic terms, the environmental and social costs of large dams have not been sufficiently taken into account.
food security in developing countries, particularly in parts of africa, should be seen as a challenge that needs to be addressed urgently. millions of people are starving and this cannot be acceptable to the european union. if we don't change this, we will be facing the threat of a global negative humanitarian and security impact. the international community's response to these problems has been slow and inadequate. eu member states need to fundamentally strengthen their participation in the transformation of humanitarian aid into aid and development policy. in particular, the development of agriculture and rural areas. in the long term, the key role will be to promote educational programmes with the widest possible access to all those who need it. the launch of these regular training programmes could serve as an effective means to help resolve this deadlock and prevent its recurrence.
food security in developing countries is literally a matter of life and death, as the current situation in africa shows. it is the union's moral duty to act and to choose the right way to help. i am in favour of european union aid being directed towards sustainable small-scale food production in order to increase food availability. agriculture continues to be the backbone of rural economies throughout the developing world. agricultural production systems need to be reworked and moved away from the current ones that are too dependent on external inputs and oil. much more attention needs to be paid to local and regional conditions. special attention should be paid to women and their needs, as they make up the majority of smallholder farmers. at the same time, i would like to draw attention to the role of speculation in commodity markets, which contributes to the rise in food prices and thus to the reduction in food availability, with disastrous consequences. this is an urgent reason why the commission should focus on financial sector regulation.
food security in developing countries is a long-term problem. recurrent famines are wiping out the population of these countries, with women and children being the most affected. i consider that the measures to ensure basic food security in developing countries in the report are an important way of ensuring that the right of local people to own agricultural land is preserved. the massive land grabbing by foreign agricultural investors leads to the spread of poverty, displacement, starvation and uncontrolled migration of the local population. weak and corrupt governments thus deny their people the right to food, to drinking water, and to food. i therefore think it is worthwhile to resume the dialogue on international rules for the acquisition of arable land. the european union, through its humanitarian policy, has the moral right to raise such a subject with the international community.
in our work we must not forget the children who live abroad with their parents and whose parents work in the european institutions, in representative offices and so on, and who have the opportunity to study in european schools. these schools not only allow them to study in their mother tongue and not lose their connection with home, but also to study other european languages and receive a top-level european education in a multicultural and multilingual environment. i'm against cutting funding for these schools, but i'm more for finding new solutions. seeking alternative sources of funding, for example from the private sector, or taking in children of parents working in other international institutions. i also call on the member states to honour their commitment to financial support for european schools and the deployment of teachers to teach their mother tongue. i also call for 100% recognition of the european baccalaureate in all member states and i call for a uniform approach to the assessment of secondary school graduates by european universities without any discrimination. in conclusion, i would like to thank the rapporteur, mr cavad, and the representatives of the european commission for their excellent cooperation.
the european union has set up a system of european schools for the children of staff of the european institutions, which are intended to enable children to receive education in their mother tongue, even where the european institutions are located. as a result of the union's recruitment policy, the number of pupils in these schools is constantly increasing, which raises problems in securing a sufficient number of qualified teachers and lecturers. in the absence of an effective mechanism to enforce the commitments made by the member states in setting up these schools, some member states do not fill the places with their seconded teachers and school management has to improvise and replace the missing teachers with tutors who are not always adequately qualified. it would therefore be good to finalise the rules for the functioning of the european schools so that they are able to fulfil their mission responsibly, as their parents rightly expect. if the union needs to save money today, let it save money on museums or on trips to strasbourg, but not on the education of its children.
the european union is also characterised by the high mobility of its staff, who naturally move with their children. it is important for every person to receive education in his or her mother tongue, and european schools are unique in this respect and their work is worthwhile. it is also important and gratifying that the european schools serve as a good pedagogical model for other types of schools. i fully support the extension of the european schools model. it is one way of building a common european identity from an early age. in this sense, i would also like to advocate that the appropriate political, administrative and financial conditions be created for european schools and their expansion. an educated nation, an educated society - that means better jobs, a better quality of life, a higher standard of living. at the same time, it is important to ensure that pupils and students receive quality information in all types of schools, including information that will increase their european awareness and provide a good basis for shared european prosperity.
as the draftsman of the opinion of the committee on employment, i would like to thank you for the excellent cooperation with the rapporteur, who set himself the objective of examining cohesion policy from the point of view of how it could be improved, what are the obstacles that prevent better use and what are the circumstances that must be improved in any case so that the use, the absorption, the use of these funds is better and more efficient. i believe that the committee on employment is primarily responsible for the european social fund, which has a very important role to play in this crisis, especially when reducing unemployment is a priority. in this connection, i think the rapporteur rightly pointed out that there is a problem with co-financing, because, as a result of austerity measures, not only governments but also local businesses and local authorities have problems in producing the means needed for co-financing.
the draining of funds from the structural funds and the cohesion fund is still causing problems, but it has also caused problems in the past for a number of countries. the complexity of the rules and conditions to be met, as well as the number of errors, lead to unintended consequences. the time spent on control and management of the funds is disproportionate. and so we have to find the balance, the right balance, between simplifying rules and procedures and making them stable. another important point to focus on is the distinction between the different forms of non-fulfilment of the conditions for drawing on the funds. i would like to advocate that, for example, formal defects be distinguished according to their seriousness. the aim of fund managers should not be to punish but to seek ways to remedy, in cooperation with beneficiaries, any formal deficiencies due to inattention or lack of capacity. a separate chapter is devoted to the use of funds to address the roma problem. i would like to say that the preparation of such funds should be seen in a completely new light in this area.
an effective union cohesion policy is a prerequisite for the harmonious development of all regions of the union, i.e. it contributes to reducing economic, social and territorial disparities. the ability to draw funds, or in other words the effective use of the funds allocated from the structural funds and the cohesion fund, varies from region to region. unfortunately, the most disadvantaged regions, which are the ones most in need of funds, often lag behind in their absorption because they lack not only the minimum financial resources needed to co-finance but also the human resources and administrative support. this administrative and institutional capacity of the public sector at national, regional and local level must be targeted. competent authorities should also consider new procedures for upskilling their staff. in conclusion, many countries have shown the ability to draw on the eu funds much more effectively than in the past. my country is an example of this, where it draws much more efficiently than the previous government that was in power before.
in my country, we have a saying that bad luck doesn't come from the mountains, but from the people. earthquakes, major floods, fires and other disasters are also common in our european countries, and the rescue teams of the affected countries are often unable, especially in the early stages of disasters, to provide the necessary assistance in the event of major disasters, and international assistance often becomes a necessity. the commission's decision to merge the monitoring and information centre with the echo crisis centre and to create a single emergency response centre ready to coordinate european union crisis humanitarian aid operations at any time and in a continuous operation is therefore to be welcomed. the establishment of this institution as a central point for the rapid coordination of european material and financial assistance would further enhance the usefulness of this institution. i am convinced that with good preparedness of mechanisms, crisis and humanitarian aid teams, we can effectively save the lives and health of our people in emergency situations.
the fact that the european union reached 25% of global gdp in 2000, when the lisbon strategy was launched, while only 18% is projected in 2020, is a clear reason for serious reflection. a sober assessment of the current state of play, reflecting the reality of today's world economy, is urgently needed to develop robust short-, medium- and long-term strategies to revive the eu economy and make it competitive. i am convinced that the conclusion of trade agreements and the opening up of the european market must not come at the expense of the safety of eu consumers and the values on which the european union is founded. i therefore reiterate that all free trade agreements should include provisions on respect for fundamental human rights and, of course, minimum environmental and social standards.
the commission's trade communication is essentially a continuation of the 2006 global europe strategy. unfortunately, the strategy is also the result of european businesses' frustration with the deadlock in which the wto's doha round of negotiations has found themselves. as it is not working at multilateral level, the european union is trying to engage in bilateral agreements, especially with countries with fast-growing economies. however, this form of trade policy of the european union is bitterly ultra-liberal and focuses almost exclusively on economic development and economic motivation. all other non-market aspects such as sustainable development, social cohesion, human rights and so on are being marginalized. however, these aspects should be prioritised and cross-cutting for all european union policies, including trade policy. and this is not just true outside the union, unfortunately. within the union itself, there is an effort to undermine social and environmental standards. i would therefore appeal to the commission not to give in to pressure and to really prepare a strategy which respects our european values.

in writing. − international air transport relations between member states and third countries are usually governed by bilateral air service agreements. the court of justice of the eu ruled in 2002 that the customary designation provisions contained in member states' bilateral air services agreements are contrary to eu law. they shall allow a third country to refuse, withdraw or suspend the authorisation or privileges of an air carrier which has been designated by a member state but which is not majority owned by that member state or its nationals and is not subject to effective control by that member state or its nationals. the commission negotiated an agreement replacing certain provisions in the 13 existing bilateral air services agreements concluded between eu member states and the united mexican states. mexico is an important market for eu carriers, with some 2.5 million passengers and 90 000 tonnes of cargo in 2009. given the size and importance of the eu-mexico air transport market, the possibility of a more comprehensive air transport agreement should be explored, which could deepen mutual cooperation on air transport issues and expand opportunities and benefits for industry and consumers in both mexico and the eu. in the light of the above, i am therefore in favour of the conclusion of this agreement.
in writing. - mexico is an important market for eu carriers, with some 2.5 million passengers a year and 90,000 tonnes of cargo. given the size and importance of the eu-mexico air transport market, the possibility of reaching a more comprehensive eu-mexico air transport agreement should be explored. such an agreement would deepen eu-mexico cooperation on air transport issues. the opportunities and benefits for industry and consumers in both mexico and the eu would be broadened. moreover, a comprehensive open airspace between the eu and the americas would be created, following the extensive agreements already concluded with the us, canada and, most recently, brazil. the aim is to provide all eu carriers with non-discriminatory access to air routes between the eu member state that has signed the bilateral agreement and mexico. the safety provisions in bilateral agreements will apply in cases where regulatory control of an air carrier is exercised by an eu member state other than the one that designated the air carrier. any practices distorting competition shall be prohibited. the agreement with mexico will restore a solid legal basis for eu-mexico relations in the field of air transport. this is an important first step in strengthening eu-mexico air transport relations.
